system:
You are a computational scientist who builds mechanistic models of biochemical and pharmacological processes from experimental data. You have no model library: write every candidate model yourself as custom code for fit_model. Work the way a careful scientist does:

1. Plan: call write_plan first with a short list of steps; update it if your approach changes.
2. Look before you fit: inspect the data and use run_python for quick numeric checks that discriminate mechanisms.
3. Hypothesise: record at least two competing hypotheses with record_hypothesis, each with what it predicts in these data. Update their status as evidence comes in.
4. Test: fit competing models with the same error model and compare BIC, residual diagnostics and identifiability. Fit independent models in the same turn to save steps.
5. Revise: if a model leaves structured residuals, work out what the data do that it does not allow, and write a better model.
6. Stay honest: always consider the simplest model, including no effect at all. Report parameters the data cannot determine. Never state a number that did not come from a tool result.
7. Submit with submit_model (mechanism_label 'custom'), citing fit_ids as evidence.

You have at most 20 model turns, so be efficient.
task_prompt:
Initial reaction rates v (uM/min) of a purified enzyme were measured at substrate concentrations S (uM) (no inhibitor, I = 0). Each condition was measured in duplicate; rates carry additive measurement noise.

The data table has 16 rows with columns: S, v. Your model will be used to predict rates within the measured substrate range.

Find the mechanistic model that best explains these data, fit it, check it critically, and submit it.

steps: Fit substrate inhibition model and compare BIC
Check residuals and submit best model

content.thinking: Only eight distinct substrate concentrations here, with some repeated, and the rates keep climbing up to S=20, looking close to linear at the high end. I'll try Michaelis-Menten and a substrate-inhibition fit, and possibly a Hill model as well.

name: fit_model
fit_model

content.thinking: The Michaelis-Menten fit gives a Vmax of 165 and Km of 857, which is nearly linear over this range, with a slope around 0.193. I'll test a simple linear model, v = k·S, and compare it against the saturating fit. The noise is around 0.11, and the S=0.5 point looks like noise, so a one-parameter linear model seems most reasonable. Next I'll fit that and check the residuals point by point.

input.custom_code:
PARAMS = ['k']
def predict(df, p):
    S = df['S'].values
    return p['k']*S

name: fit_model

content.thinking:
The linear model wins on BIC, and the data show no saturation up to 20 µM, so the linear regime is the working limit. Substrate inhibition is ruled out because its Ksi fit runs to infinity. I'm leaning toward submitting the linear rate fit and weighing whether to skip the hypothesis record to save turns.

I'm still weighing whether to batch the hypothesis records into a single call to save turns, since each one is a separate call anyway.

fit2: Ksi diverges (1.4e17), i.e. no inhibition signal; BIC -64.4 vs -69.8 for linear.

input.summary: Rates are proportional to substrate across 0.5-20 uM: v = k*S with k = 0.1896 (SE 1%), additive sigma 0.107 (fit4). This one-parameter linear model has the lowest AIC/BIC (-70.6/-69.8) of the candidates, with no residual structure (runs z=0.07). Michaelis-Menten (fit1) collapses to the same linear regime with Vmax and Km unidentifiable (Km ~857 uM, r=+1.000), so saturation is not detectable in this range. Substrate inhibition (fit2) gives no signal (Ksi diverges), and the Hill exponent (fit3) is ~0.98, so no cooperativity is needed.
nonidentifiable_params: Vmax and Km of Michaelis-Menten separately (only Vmax/Km ~0.19 is determined)
